newsitem.title: TURKEY: Amnesty accuses Turkey of gross rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty accuses Turkey of gross rights abuses.

text.p: Amnesty International on Tuesday accused Turkey's powerful security forces of committing gross human rights abuses knowing that the civilian authorities would rarely challenge them.

Political leaders, the judiciary and even doctors turned a blind eye to torture, extrajudicial killings and the recent phenomenon of suspects "disappearing" in police custody, the London-based human rights group said in a report.

"Turkey's persistent record of gross human rights violations results from a complete disregard at the highest level for international human rights standards and Turkey's own laws protecting human rights," it said.
The report kicked off a six-month Amnesty campaign to focus internatonal attention on abuses in Turkey.

There was no immediate comment from the Turkish government on the report. Turkey has rejected international criticism of its human rights record in the past and accuses Amnesty of bias in singling out Turkey for criticism.

Most complaints of rights violations occur in the mainly Kurdish southeast where security forces and separatist rebels have been locked in a bitter conflict for the past 12 years. More than 20,000 people have died in the fighting.

"During the first interrogation they grabbed me by the hair and punched my head against the wall," Amnesty quoted suspected rebel sympathiser Nuray Sen as saying of her 10-day questioning by police last year.

"They kicked me and one officer put his boot into my mouth...I was spitting blood. They pressed a wooden truncheon against my genitals and twisted it. They laughed, saying: 'She is enjoying this'," the report quoted her as saying.
Sen found the battered body of her husband Mehmet in a hospital morgue in 1994 after he was detained by police, it said.

Amnesty also accused the separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) of rights violations, saying its guerrillas had killed at least 400 prisoners and civilians between 1993 and 1995 and 90 teachers since 1984.

More than 100 people, mostly Kurdish villagers, have "disappeared" in police custody since 1993 and over 1,000 civilians suspected of pro-rebel activity had been killed in the last five years, the report said.
It quotes an unnamed villager who survived a death squad attack in Bitlis province in 1994 in which two of his relatives died. His village had refused to joined an anti-rebel militia.

"They took us to a piece of waste ground and then they opened fire on us. My brother and my uncle fell to the ground...I lay on the ground and pretended to be dead. They went back to the other two and fired a couple of shots," he said.
Amnesty said torture, including electric shocks, beatings on the genitals and spraying detainees with high-pressure hoses, was widespread throughout the country.
Children and suspects detained for common crime -- as opposed to political militants -- were also liable to be tortured, Amnesty said.

It said Turkish judges and prosecutors frequently failed to act on complaints of torture by detainees and doctors were often coerced into writing medical reports that hid evidence of torture or illegal killing.
